title: No. 17 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: An objection of a different kind from the one stated and answered in my last address may perhaps also be raised against the principle of legislation for the individual citizens of America. It may be said that the principle would tend to make the government of the Union too powerful, and let it swallow up the residual authorities that it might be thought proper to leave with the States for local purposes. I give the love of power all the room that any reasonable man could ask. Even so, I confess I cannot see what temptation the persons entrusted with administering the general government could ever feel to strip the States of authorities of that kind. Regulating the mere domestic police of a State seems to me to hold out little to attract ambition. Commerce, finance, negotiation, and war seem to cover every object that has charms for minds ruled by that passion, and all the powers needed for those objects ought, in the first instance, to be placed in the national depository. Administering private justice between citizens of the same State, supervising agriculture, and the other concerns of a similar nature are all things properly provided for by local legislation. They can never be desirable cares for a general jurisdiction. It is therefore unlikely that the federal councils would be inclined to usurp the powers connected with them. Trying to exercise those powers would be as troublesome as it would be useless, and for that reason possessing them would add nothing to the dignity, the importance, or the splendor of the national government.

But grant, for the sake of argument, that mere wantonness and lust of domination would be enough to produce that inclination. Even so, we may safely affirm that the will of the constituent body of the national representatives, in other words the people of the individual States, would hold so extravagant an appetite in check. It will always be far easier for the State governments to encroach on the national authorities than for the national government to encroach on the State authorities. The proof of this proposition rests on the greater influence the State governments will generally have over the people, provided they administer their affairs with uprightness and prudence. This fact also teaches us that all federal constitutions have an inherent and intrinsic weakness, and that we cannot take too much care in organizing them to give them all the force compatible with the principles of liberty.

The State governments would have the greater influence partly because the national government is spread out, but chiefly because of the nature of the objects that the State administrations would attend to.

It is a known fact about human nature that its affections are generally weak in proportion to the distance or diffuseness of their object. A man is more attached to his family than to his neighborhood, and to his neighborhood than to the community at large. By the same principle, the people of each State would tend to feel a stronger bias toward their local governments than toward the government of the Union. The one exception would be if a much better administration of the Union's government overcame the force of that principle.
This strong propensity of the human heart would find powerful allies in the objects of State regulation.

The State governments will necessarily supervise a variety of smaller interests, which will form so many rivulets of influence running through every part of society. To list them would take a detail too tedious and uninteresting to be worth the instruction it might give.

There is one transcendent advantage belonging to the province of the State governments that by itself puts the matter in a clear and satisfactory light. I mean the ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice. Of all things, this is the most powerful, the most universal, and the most attractive source of popular obedience and attachment. Justice is the immediate and visible guardian of life and property. Its benefits and its terrors are constantly at work before the public eye. It regulates all those personal interests and familiar concerns to which individuals are most immediately alive. For these reasons it does more than anything else to impress on the minds of the people affection, esteem, and reverence toward the government. This great cement of society will flow almost entirely through the channels of the particular governments. Quite apart from all other causes of influence, it would give them so decided a hold over their respective citizens that they would always be a complete counterpoise to the power of the Union and, not infrequently, dangerous rivals to it.

The operations of the national government, by contrast, come less directly under the eyes of the mass of citizens. Its benefits will be noticed and attended to chiefly by speculative men. Since it deals with more general interests, it will be less likely to come home to the feelings of the people, and to the same degree less likely to inspire a habitual sense of obligation and an active feeling of attachment.
The experience of all the federal constitutions we know of, and of all others bearing the least resemblance to them, has borne out the reasoning on this point abundantly.

The ancient feudal systems were not, strictly speaking, confederacies, but they shared the nature of that kind of association. There was a common head, chieftain, or sovereign, whose authority reached over the whole nation. There were also a number of subordinate vassals, or feudatories, who were allotted large portions of land. Under them were numerous trains of INFERIOR vassals or retainers, who occupied and farmed that land on the tenure of fealty or obedience to the persons from whom they held it. Each principal vassal was a kind of sovereign within his own domains. The result was continual opposition to the sovereign's authority and frequent wars among the great barons, or chief feudatories, themselves. The power of the head of the nation was commonly too weak either to keep the public peace or to protect the people against the oppressions of their immediate lords. Historians emphatically call this period of European history the times of feudal anarchy.

A sovereign of vigorous and warlike temper and superior abilities would gain a personal weight and influence that served, for a time, in place of a more regular authority. In general, however, the power of the barons triumphed over that of the prince. In many instances his dominion was thrown off entirely and the great fiefs were set up as independent principalities or States. In the instances where the monarch finally prevailed over his vassals, his success was chiefly owing to the vassals' tyranny over their dependents. The barons, or nobles, were equally the enemies of the sovereign and the oppressors of the common people, and were dreaded and detested by both. At length mutual danger and mutual interest brought about a union between the two that was fatal to the power of the aristocracy. If the nobles had instead kept the fidelity and devotion of their retainers and followers by acting with mercy and justice, their contests with the prince must almost always have ended in their favor, and in the reduction or overthrow of the royal authority.

This assertion is not founded merely on speculation or conjecture. Among other illustrations of its truth that might be cited, Scotland furnishes a compelling example. The spirit of clanship was introduced into that kingdom at an early date and bound the nobles and their dependents together by ties equal to those of kinship. This made the aristocracy a constant overmatch for the power of the monarch. It remained so until the union with England subdued its fierce and ungovernable spirit and brought it within the rules of subordination that a more rational and more energetic system of civil government had earlier established in the latter kingdom.

The separate governments in a confederacy may fittingly be compared to the feudal baronies. They have this advantage on their side. For the reasons already explained, they will generally have the confidence and good will of the people. With so important a support, they will be able to oppose effectively all encroachments by the national government. It will be well if they are not able to counteract its legitimate and necessary authority. The points of similarity are the rivalry of power that applies to both, and the CONCENTRATION of large portions of the community's strength in particular DEPOSITORIES. In the one case these are at the disposal of individuals; in the other, at the disposal of political bodies.

A concise review of the events that have attended confederate governments will further illustrate this important doctrine. Inattention to it has been the great source of our political mistakes and has aimed our jealousy at the wrong target. This review will be the subject of some ensuing papers.
